z-m-02-01.title: Two pencils we did not lay side by side: which is longer?
z-m-02-01.topic: Chaining length comparisons and judging whether there is enough information
z-m-02-01.goal: Tell apart when you can chain together comparison results you already have and when you need to compare more, and say what more to compare to settle it.
z-m-02-01.material: There are four new pencils on the group's desk. The name tags are 가, 나, 다, and 라. To compare lengths, all the pencils are straightened and lined up with one end matched. So far, only two comparisons have been made side by side. First, 가 is longer than 나. Second, 나 is longer than 다. 가 and 다 have not been put side by side, and 라 has not yet been put next to any pencil.
z-m-02-01.thinking.0: Chaining comparisons you already know to reach a new conclusion
z-m-02-01.thinking.1: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-02-01.thinking.2: Choosing the next comparison needed to decide
z-m-02-01.prereq.0: Comparing 'longer/shorter' by putting two things end to end (Grade 1 level)
z-m-02-01.s.s1.prompt: 가 and 다 have not been put side by side. Which of the two pencils can we say is longer?
z-m-02-01.s.s1.hint.0: Line up 가, 나, 다 from longest to shortest and write them down.
z-m-02-01.s.s1.hint.1: In the line, compare the places of 가 and 다.
z-m-02-01.s.s1.o.a: We cannot know yet. We have to put the two side by side
z-m-02-01.s.s1.o.b: 다 is longer. 다 is the last pencil that came up
z-m-02-01.s.s1.r.b: The order in which the pencils came up in the story has nothing to do with length. Only the comparisons that said which pencil is longer count as evidence.
z-m-02-01.s.s1.o.c: 가 is longer. We can know by chaining the comparisons
z-m-02-01.s.s1.r.c: This chained the two comparisons: 가 is longer than 나, and 나 is longer than 다.
z-m-02-01.s.s1.o.d: They are the same length. Because we did not put them side by side
z-m-02-01.s.s1.r.d: Not having put them side by side is not evidence that the lengths are the same. Whether they are the same or different must be said from the results of comparing.
z-m-02-01.s.s2.prompt: New information: we put 다 and 라 side by side, and 라 was longer than 다. Then which is longer, 가 or 라?
z-m-02-01.s.s2.hint.0: Line up 가, 나, 다, 라 from longest to shortest. Draw two or more possible lines.
z-m-02-01.s.s2.hint.1: Move 라's place around and check that the two known comparisons and the new comparison are all kept.
z-m-02-01.s.s2.o.a: 가 is longer. 가 is the pencil that came up first
z-m-02-01.s.s2.r.a: Being the first pencil to come up is not a reason about length. You need to look at whether there is a comparison that connects 가 and 라.
z-m-02-01.s.s2.o.b: We do not know yet. There is no comparison that connects 가 and 라
z-m-02-01.s.s2.o.c: We cannot tell. We have to put 가 and 다 side by side again first
z-m-02-01.s.s2.r.c: It has already been decided that 가 is longer than 다. What is not decided now is between 가 and 라.
z-m-02-01.s.s2.o.d: 라 is longer. Because it is the comparison we learned last
z-m-02-01.s.s2.r.d: You cannot say it is longer because it is the comparison we learned later. We only learned that 라 is longer than 다.
z-m-02-01.s.s2.explain: We only know that both 가 and 라 are longer than 다. Even if both are longer than 다, this comparison alone does not decide which of 가 and 라 is longer. We need to put 가 and 라 side by side, or have another comparison that connects the two.
z-m-02-01.s.s3.prompt: Which two pencils could you put side by side to find out whether 라 is longer than 가? Write one way, and also write what result would let you know.
z-m-02-01.s.s3.hint.0: First check whether the known comparisons directly connect 가 and 라.
z-m-02-01.s.s3.hint.1: Decide to put 라 next to one of 가, 나, 다, and think separately about when 라 is longer and when it is shorter.
z-m-02-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: If you put the two pencils I chose side by side, is it decided which of 가 and 라 is longer?
z-m-02-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you work out whether there are results where we still would not know?
z-m-02-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you notice, as in model answer 2, that there is also a way of adding a condition, saying 'we can know only when the result is like this'?
z-m-02-01.s.s3.model.0: Put 라 and 가 side by side. If you compare the lengths of the two pencils directly, you can tell right away which is longer.
z-m-02-01.s.s3.model.1: Put 라 next to 나. If 라 is shorter than 나, 가 is longer than 나, so you can know that 가 is longer. If 라 is longer than 나, we still do not know.
z-m-02-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer also says that, depending on the result, it may be decided or we may still not know.
z-m-02-01.s.s1.r.a: It is true that trying it directly gives a sure answer. But before saying "we can't know yet", see whether you can chain together the two comparisons you already know.
z-m-02-01.s.s1.explain: Ga is longer than Na, and Na is longer than Da. Lined up from longest, Ga comes first, then Na, then Da. So Ga is longer than Da. You can check by trying directly, but even before trying, you can find out by chaining the comparisons you already know.

z-m-02-02.title: Crossing the stepping stones: is there only one way?
z-m-02-02.topic: Many ways to make a set distance with jumps of 1 step and 2 steps
z-m-02-02.goal: Show by making them yourself that there are many ways to cover a set distance with two kinds of jumps, and say how the number of one kind of jump changes when the number of the other kind changes.
z-m-02-02.material: There are stepping stones laid across a stream. It is exactly 6 steps from where you start to the other side. In one jump you can only jump forward 1 step or 2 steps. You do not jump backward or jump past 6 steps. You have crossed only if you land exactly on the other side. Yoona said, 'It is 6 steps, so the only way is to jump 1 step 6 times.'
z-m-02-02.thinking.0: Testing whether there are many ways
z-m-02-02.thinking.1: Finding the possible ways within a condition (a limit on the number of jumps)
z-m-02-02.thinking.2: Working out the swapping relationship between the two kinds of jumps
z-m-02-02.prereq.1: Counting on by 1 step and 2 steps (Grade 1 to 2 level)
z-m-02-02.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about what Yoona said, 'The only way to cross is jumping 1 step 6 times'?
z-m-02-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write down jumping 1 step 6 times as one way, then change it by putting in one 2-step jump so it is still 6 steps.
z-m-02-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write the number of steps for each jump in order and count to check how many steps there are in all.
z-m-02-02.s.s1.o.a: That's right. Jumping 1 step 6 times fits exactly, so there is no other way
z-m-02-02.s.s1.r.a: Finding one way that fits exactly does not mean there is no other way. You did not test whether you may mix in 2-step jumps.
z-m-02-02.s.s1.o.b: There are two ways. Jump only 1 step at a time, or jump only 2 steps at a time
z-m-02-02.s.s1.r.b: You found the ways of jumping only 1 step and only 2 steps. You did not check whether there are ways that mix the two kinds of jumps.
z-m-02-02.s.s1.o.c: We do not know yet. We need to know the size of each stepping stone
z-m-02-02.s.s1.r.c: You can work out the ways with just the number of steps, no matter how big the stones are. If you write down the order of jumps yourself, you can find out.
z-m-02-02.s.s1.o.d: It is not just one way. You may mix in 2-step jumps
z-m-02-02.s.s1.explain: For example, jumping 2 steps, 2 steps, 1 step, 1 step also adds up to 6 steps. If you mix 1-step jumps and 2-step jumps, there are more ways to cross.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to cross 6 steps with 5 jumps or fewer in all. Make 2 different ways to cross by jumping 1 step a times and 2 steps b times.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the number of 2-step jumps, b, then work out how many 1-step jumps you need to fill the remaining steps.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.hint.1: With the a and b you chose, calculate the number of steps jumped and the number of jumps separately, and check that they fit the conditions.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of jumps is a natural number, 0 or more.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of jumps must be a natural number that is 0 or more, like 0, 1, 2, ....
z-m-02-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The distance jumped is exactly 6 steps.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The distance jumped is not 6 steps. Count how many steps in all you went with the 1-step jumps and 2-step jumps.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of jumps is 5 or fewer.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of jumps is more than 5.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.explain: If a=4, b=1, then 1 step 4 times and 2 steps 1 time make 6 steps, and it is 5 jumps. a=2, b=2 is 4 jumps, and a=0, b=3 is 3 jumps. Jumping 1 step 6 times (a=6, b=0) is 6 jumps, so it is left out because of the limit on jumps.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare 2 ways. When the 2-step jumps go up by one, how do the 1-step jumps change? Also write the reason in one sentence.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Count how much a changed when b went up by one.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: When the 2-step jumps go up by one, ...
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is what I wrote based on the a and b of the two ways I made?
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give the reason that '2 steps once is the same distance as 1 step twice'?
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the same thing happens with two other ways?
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.model.0: When the 2-step jumps go up by one, the 1-step jumps go down by two. This is because 2 steps is the same distance as 1 step twice.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.model.1: If you jump 2 steps one more time, you can jump 1 step two fewer times and still get 6 steps. 2 steps once and 1 step twice are the same, so they can be swapped.
z-m-02-02.s.s3.prompt: This time, you decided to allow 3 jumps or fewer. How many ways are there to cross exactly 6 steps?
z-m-02-02.s.s3.hint.0: Count the jumps again for each way you made before and keep only the ones with 3 jumps or fewer.
z-m-02-02.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how many steps you must jump on average each time to go 6 steps in 3 jumps.
z-m-02-02.s.s3.o.a: One way. Jump 2 steps only, 3 times
z-m-02-02.s.s3.o.b: Three ways. It is the same as when it was 5 or fewer
z-m-02-02.s.s3.r.b: The limit on jumps got stricter. Of the ways you made when it was 5 or fewer, the ones with more than 3 jumps must be dropped.
z-m-02-02.s.s3.o.c: Two ways. 2 steps 3 times, and 2 steps 2 times with 1 step 2 times
z-m-02-02.s.s3.r.c: 2 steps twice with 1 step twice is 4 jumps in all. Count whether that fits within 3 or fewer.
z-m-02-02.s.s3.o.d: None. You cannot cross 6 steps in 3 jumps
z-m-02-02.s.s3.r.d: First calculate whether you can get there in 3 jumps by jumping 2 steps each time.
z-m-02-02.s.s3.explain: To jump 6 steps in 3 jumps or fewer, the only way is to jump 2 steps 3 times. The (a=2, b=2) and (a=4, b=1) found before are 4 jumps and 5 jumps, so they are dropped. When a new condition appears, the number of ways can change.
z-m-02-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the a and b of the two methods you made side by side.

z-m-02-03.title: If they each get the same number of stickers more, who has how many more?
z-m-02-03.topic: Seeing whether the difference between two numbers stays the same when you add the same number
z-m-02-03.goal: Test with numbers when you can judge knowing only the difference, even without the starting numbers, and tell apart adding equally to both sides from adding to only one side.
z-m-02-03.material: Jihu and Hayun collect stickers. Read the story below one step at a time and say what you think.
z-m-02-03.thinking.0: Deciding how to judge when you do not know the numbers
z-m-02-03.thinking.1: Testing a judgment by putting in numbers
z-m-02-03.thinking.2: Working out whether the conclusion changes when the condition changes
z-m-02-03.prereq.0: Addition and subtraction of numbers up to 20
z-m-02-03.s.s1.prompt: The information opens up one piece at a time. At each step, choose what you think fits best and go to the next step.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.hint.0: Pick small numbers for the two children's stickers and show them with a picture or a table.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.hint.1: From the numbers you picked, count what the difference between the two children becomes after each gets 2.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Jihu has 3 more stickers than Hayun. We do not know yet how many each of them had at the start.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: If the teacher gives both of them 2 more stickers each, how many more stickers will Jihu have than Hayun?
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.after: We do not know the numbers yet, so being careful and saying 'we cannot tell' is reasonable with this information, and so is guessing 'the difference might stay the same'. Let's test it by putting in numbers.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You thought 3 plus the 2 received makes 5. Think also about the fact that both of them received 2 each.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We cannot tell yet. We need to know how many they had at the start
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You said it carefully because we do not know how many each has. If you test with numbers, you can check whether you really need to know.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You guessed that since the number received is the same, the difference will stay the same too. It is a guess worth testing with numbers.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It seems you found the difference between 3 and 2. Read again that both of them received the 2.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Now we know the starting numbers. Jihu had 7 stickers and Hayun had 4. The teacher gave each 2, so Jihu has 9 and Hayun has 6.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how many more stickers does Jihu have than Hayun? Compare with what you thought at first.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The difference between 7 and 4 is 3, and the difference between 9 and 6 is also 3. If you said 'we cannot tell' at first, you now learned that in this example the difference stayed the same. We have only checked it with these two numbers, so let's think about other cases too.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You may have compared a number from before receiving with a number after receiving, mixing them. Compare the two numbers from the same time.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You may have thought the 2 stickers received became the difference. Compare 9 and 6 directly.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The difference between 9 and 6 is also the same as the difference between 7 and 4 before receiving.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: 9 and 6 are different numbers. Count again which one is more and by how many.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.info: This is a story about two other children. Seou has 3 more stickers than Gaon. We do not know how many each has. This time the teacher gave 4 more stickers to Gaon only.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Who has more, Seou or Gaon, and how many more?
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.after: When Gaon gets 4, he catches up with all of the 3-sticker difference from Seou and has 1 left over. For example, if Seou has 5 and Gaon has 2, and only Gaon gets 4, then it is 5 and 6. Even if you do not know how many each has, you can judge using the difference and the number received.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You added 4 to 3. Think about the fact that the one who received the 4 is Gaon, not Seou.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The difference went from 3 to 1. Look at whether the 4 received is greater or less than 3.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: We cannot tell. We do not know how many each has
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: As you saw earlier when you put in numbers, even if you do not know how many, there are times you can judge knowing only the difference. This time too, test by putting in small numbers.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is the idea that Gaon caught up with all of Seou's 3-sticker lead and has 1 more.
z-m-02-03.s.s1.reflect: At first you may have felt 'we cannot tell'. When you put in numbers, there were times when you only needed the difference. When both are given the same amount, the difference stays the same, but when only one side is given, it changed. Say at which step and how your thinking changed, or whether it did not change.
z-m-02-03.s.s2.prompt: In the example of Jihu and Hayun (7 and 4), write using numbers why the difference stays the same even when they each get 2. Also add briefly what happens if only one of them is given.
z-m-02-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write the difference between 9 and 6 next to the difference between 7 and 4 and compare.
z-m-02-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate yourself what happens to Hayun's number and the difference if only Hayun is given 2.
z-m-02-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it writing where I checked the difference myself with the numbers I wrote (7, 4, 9, 6, etc.)?
z-m-02-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you give as the reason that the two children increased 'by the same amount'?
z-m-02-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you also say that when only one side is given, the difference changes?
z-m-02-03.s.s2.model.0: From 7 and 4, if both get 2, it becomes 9 and 6, so the difference stays 3. Both increased by the same amount, so the 3 that Jihu was ahead by does not change. If only Hayun is given, the difference gets smaller.
z-m-02-03.s.s2.model.1: If you see Jihu as having Hayun's 4 plus 3 more, then even when each is given 2, Jihu still has 3 more than Hayun. If only one side is given, the 3 changes.

z-m-02-04.topic: Looking at how the number added changes when a step is added
z-m-02-04.goal: Work out whether one observation is enough to say 'it keeps going up by the same number', state the rule from further counting, and guess the next case.
z-m-02-04.thinking.0: Stopping before generalizing from one example
z-m-02-04.thinking.1: Counting more cases to collect evidence
z-m-02-04.thinking.2: Guessing the next case with the rule you found
z-m-02-04.prereq.1: Counting blocks to see how the numbers grow
z-m-02-04.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Doyun's claim based on only the 1-step and 2-step stairs seen so far?
z-m-02-04.s.s1.r.a: You looked at going from 1 step to 2 steps just once and said it will keep going that way. You have not counted whether 3 steps and 4 steps do the same.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.explain: Doyun looked only once, at going from 1 step to 2 steps. It is hard to say 'keeps going' from just one observation, so if you add more steps like 3 and 4 and count, you can tell whether the claim is right.
z-m-02-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of blocks for 1 step through 4 steps in one line, and write the number added between each pair of neighboring numbers.
z-m-02-04.s.s2.hint.1: Look at the numbers added side by side and compare whether they are the same or different.
z-m-02-04.s.s3.prompt: What would you say to Doyun? Use numbers to tell Doyun whether his claim is right, and also guess how many blocks a 5-step stair would have.
z-m-02-04.s.s3.hint.0: Bring in the numbers you counted and separate the part of Doyun's claim that is right from the part that is not.
z-m-02-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did the guess for 5 steps come from the rule above, or is it a number you just picked?
z-m-02-04.title: Square Blocks: Does It Grow by the Same Number Each Time a Level Is Added?
z-m-02-04.material: You build a square shape with blocks. A 1-level one has 1 block. A 2-level one places blocks 2 across and 2 rows down, 4 in all. The 3-level and 4-level ones are built in the same way. Doyun said, "1 level has 1 and 2 levels has 4. Each time a level is added, blocks grow by 3!"
z-m-02-04.s.s1.hint.0: First build the 1-level and 2-level with blocks or a drawing.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.hint.1: Build the 3-level in the same way and count all the blocks.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.o.a: Correct. It will keep growing by 3 from now on.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.o.b: Wrong. When a level is added, blocks always grow by 4.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.r.b: They decided on a different rule without counting. If you count the 3-level and 4-level, you can tell which statement is right.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.o.c: We don't know yet. We have to count all the way to 100 levels to know.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.r.c: You don't have to go that far; by counting a few more levels, you can tell whether the statement breaks.
z-m-02-04.s.s1.o.d: We don't know yet. We have to count the blocks of the 3-level and 4-level too.
z-m-02-04.s.s2.prompt: When counted, the 3-level has 9 blocks and the 4-level has 16. If you write in order the number of blocks added going from 1 level to 2 levels, 2 to 3, and 3 to 4, what do you get?
z-m-02-04.s.s2.r.a: If you follow Doyun's words exactly, this is what happens. Check whether it matches 9 for the 3-level and 16 for the 4-level.
z-m-02-04.s.s2.r.b: You may have read each level's total as the number added. Find the difference between the earlier level and the later level.
z-m-02-04.s.s2.r.d: Find again the difference between 4 for the 2-level and 9 for the 3-level.
z-m-02-04.s.s2.explain: It grows by 3 from 1 to 4, by 5 from 4 to 9, and by 7 from 9 to 16. The numbers added grow as 3, 5, 7, so they differ from Doyun's "always 3".
z-m-02-04.s.s3.hint.1: Look at how the numbers added have changed, guess the next number to be added, and find the number of blocks in the 5-level.
z-m-02-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you state why Doyun's statement breaks using the numbers you counted (3, 5, 7)?
z-m-02-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you check whether your guess is right by actually laying out the 5-level?
z-m-02-04.s.s3.model.0: No. It grows by 3 from 1 level to 2, by 5 from 2 to 3, and by 7 from 3 to 4, so the numbers added keep getting bigger. For 5 levels, it would probably be 16 plus 9, which is 25.
z-m-02-04.s.s3.model.1: The 5-level is 5 across and 5 rows, so it would be 25. It doesn't grow by the same number every time.
z-m-02-04.s.s3.model.2: The 3-level is 9 and the 4-level is 16, so it isn't 3 at a time; it grows by 5 and then 7. The 5-level is 16+9=25.

z-m-02-05.title: The locker number rule: where is Seoyun's explanation wrong?
z-m-02-05.topic: Looking at how the top and bottom numbers pair up in a two-row number chart
z-m-02-05.goal: Check whether a statement that is true only for the first square is true for every square, find the wrong line and the wrong line that followed because of it, and rewrite it correctly.
z-m-02-05.material: The lockers at the back of the classroom have numbers on them. The top row, from the left, is locker 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and the bottom row, from the left, is locker 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The squares line up vertically: right below locker 1 in the top row is locker 2, right below locker 3 is locker 4, and so on. If you go further right, the top row continues with 11, 13, and the bottom row continues in the same way. Seoyun explained the rule of the numbers like this.
z-m-02-05.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in an explanation
z-m-02-05.thinking.1: Telling apart examples that fit and examples that break the claim (counterexamples)
z-m-02-05.thinking.2: Rewriting it as the correct rule
z-m-02-05.prereq.0: Counting on by 1s and 2s with numbers up to 20
z-m-02-05.prereq.1: Finding out how much greater one number is than another
z-m-02-05.s.s1.prompt: Pick one wrong line in Seoyun's explanation.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the two numbers that face each other vertically, one pair for each square.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.hint.1: Test Seoyun's statement against each pair you wrote, one by one.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.line.0: In the top row, each time you go one square to the right, the number goes up by 2.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.line.1: In the bottom row too, each time you go one square to the right, the number goes up by 2.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.line.2: Below locker 1 in the top row is locker 2, and below locker 3 is locker 4.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.line.3: So the bottom number is always double the top number.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.line.4: So right below locker 11 in the top row is locker 22.
z-m-02-05.s.s1.explain: The wrong line is line 4. Locker 2 below locker 1 is double, but locker 4 below locker 3 is not 6, which is double 3. It looked at only the first square being right and stretched it to every square. Line 5 is wrong too, because it followed from trusting line 4. Lines 1 to 3 are right because they are what was checked square by square.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the pairs of squares that show Seoyun's line 4 is not right.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.hint.0: For each pair, write double the top number as Seoyun said and compare it with the bottom number.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.hint.1: Mark which pairs do not come out equal to the bottom number.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.r.a: Double 3 is 6, but the bottom number is 4. You found a square where the claim breaks.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.r.b: This is a square where Seoyun's statement fits. Even if there are examples that fit, other squares can break the word 'always'.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.r.c: Double 5 is 10, but the bottom number is 6. You found a square where the claim breaks.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.r.d: Double 9 is 18, but the bottom number is 10. You found a square where the claim breaks.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.explain: In the pairs 3 and 4, 5 and 6, and 9 and 10, the bottom number is not double the top number, so Seoyun's statement breaks. Only the pair 1 and 2 fits. Having one example that fits does not make 'always' true, and one example that breaks it is enough.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.acc.0: Lockers 3 and 4 alone are enough to break Seoyun's statement. Also look for whether there are more squares that break it in the same way.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.acc.1: Lockers 5 and 6 alone are a good enough counterexample. Check whether the other pairs are the same.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.acc.2: Lockers 9 and 10 alone are a good enough counterexample. Check whether the other pairs are the same.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.acc.3: All the pairs you chose are counterexamples. Check whether lockers 9 and 10 are the same too.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.acc.4: All the pairs you chose are counterexamples. Check whether lockers 5 and 6 are the same too.
z-m-02-05.s.s2.acc.5: All the pairs you chose are counterexamples. Check whether lockers 3 and 4 are the same too.
z-m-02-05.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Seoyun's line 4 correctly, then use your fixed statement to find the number right below locker 11 in the top row.
z-m-02-05.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one pair that is vertically matched and write how much greater the bottom number is than the top number.
z-m-02-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check that the bottom number is greater by the same amount in pairs other than the one you chose, then apply it to 11.
z-m-02-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that your fixed statement is right in the pairs 1 and 2, 3 and 4, and 5 and 6?
z-m-02-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you get the number below 11 from your fixed statement?
z-m-02-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also try your fixed statement on other top numbers (for example, 7 and 13)?
z-m-02-05.s.s3.model.0: The bottom number is 1 greater than the top number. So right below 11 is 12.
z-m-02-05.s.s3.model.1: The bottom number is the number right above it plus 1. So it is 12, the number after 11.

z-m-02-06.title: The magic box that gave 4 when I put in 2
z-m-02-06.topic: Choosing test numbers to tell apart the rules of an input-output box
z-m-02-06.goal: Learn that more than one rule can fit a single result, then choose for yourself test numbers that tell two rules apart and say why.
z-m-02-06.material: When you put a number into the magic box, a new number comes out by some rule. If you put in the same number, the same number always comes out. We do not know the rule, but when 2 was put in, 4 came out. Hajun said, 'It is a box that adds 2 to the number you put in,' and Seoa said, 'It is a box that adds the number you put in twice.' For example, if you put in 3, it adds 3 and 3. The numbers you put in are natural numbers that are 0 or more, like 0, 1, 2, ....
z-m-02-06.thinking.0: Not deciding the rule from one result
z-m-02-06.thinking.1: Designing a test to tell candidate rules apart
z-m-02-06.thinking.2: Narrowing the candidates with a new result
z-m-02-06.prereq.1: Adding the same number twice (for example, 3+3)
z-m-02-06.s.s1.prompt: If you put 3 into this box, what number comes out?
z-m-02-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write the result of putting in 3 using Hajun's rule.
z-m-02-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write the result of putting in 3 using Seoa's rule, then compare the two results.
z-m-02-06.s.s1.o.a: 5 comes out. Because it adds 2 to the number put in
z-m-02-06.s.s1.r.a: You decided by trusting only Hajun's rule. Seoa's rule also fits 4 coming out when 2 was put in, but then putting in 3 gives 6.
z-m-02-06.s.s1.o.b: 6 comes out. Because it adds the number put in twice
z-m-02-06.s.s1.r.b: You decided by trusting only Seoa's rule. Hajun's rule also fits 4 coming out when 2 was put in, but then putting in 3 gives 5.
z-m-02-06.s.s1.o.c: 4 comes out. Because the box always gives the same number
z-m-02-06.s.s1.r.c: That means the same number comes out when you put in the same number. 3 is a different number from 2.
z-m-02-06.s.s1.o.d: 5 or 6 could come out. We cannot decide on one
z-m-02-06.s.s1.o.e: We cannot tell. We know nothing until we open the box
z-m-02-06.s.s1.r.e: You can find out by putting in other numbers. Even now there are the candidates Hajun's and Seoa's rules.
z-m-02-06.s.s1.explain: 4 coming out when 2 was put in fits both 'add 2' and 'add twice'. If you put in 3, the first rule gives 5 and the second rule gives 6. There may be other rules too, so for now we cannot decide on one.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose 3 different numbers to put into the box so you can tell which is the rule, Hajun's or Seoa's. The number x you put in is a natural number from 0 to 20, and it must be a number for which the two rules give different results.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.hint.0: Put each number you chose into Hajun's rule and Seoa's rule and write the numbers that come out.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.hint.1: Leave out the numbers for which the two results come out the same, and pick other numbers.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 0 to 20.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 0 to 20.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.ok.c2: If you put in this number, the results of the two rules are different.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.fail.c2: If you put in this number, the two rules give the same number, so you cannot tell which one it is.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.explain: If you put in 2, both rules give 4, so they could not be told apart already. If you put in 1, the first rule gives 3 and the second rule gives 2, so they differ. Every number except 2 works as a test that tells them apart.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Why didn't the 2 you tried at first tell the two rules apart? And write the numbers the two rules give when you put in one number you chose.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the results of putting 2 into Hajun's rule and Seoa's rule.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put the number you chose into the two rules in the same way and compare the results.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: 2 is ... the number I chose ...
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say that if you put in 2, the two rules give the same number?
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you show with numbers that, for the number I chose, the result of Hajun's rule and the result of Seoa's rule are different?
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether it is enough to name just one number, and whether naming a few more makes you more confident?
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.model.0: For 2, adding 2 gives 4 and adding twice gives 4, so they are the same. If you put in 1, Hajun's rule gives 3 and Seoa's rule gives 2, so they differ.
z-m-02-06.s.s2.because.model.1: When I put in 2, both rules gave the same number, 4, so I could not tell them apart. If I put in 5, it splits into 7 or 10.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the result of putting 4 into Seoa's rule and compare it with 6.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.hint.1: Also write the result of putting 4 into Hajun's rule and compare it with 6.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.o.a: Seoa's rule is right. Because you add 4 twice
z-m-02-06.s.s3.r.a: With Seoa's rule, when you put in 4, 8, which is 4 and 4 added, should come out.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.o.b: Hajun's rule is definitely right. There is no other rule
z-m-02-06.s.s3.r.b: A result that fits Hajun's rule came out, but you cannot say there is no other rule that gives the same result. The more times you test, the more your confidence grows.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.o.c: It is not Seoa's rule. Hajun's rule is still left
z-m-02-06.s.s3.r.d: With Hajun's rule, putting in 4 gives 4 plus 2, which is 6. Calculate again and check whether it matches the result.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.explain: With Seoa's rule, putting in 4 gives 8, which does not match 6. With Hajun's rule it becomes 6, which matches. But another rule might give the same result, so to say 'definitely' you need to test more numbers.
z-m-02-06.s.s3.prompt: You tried putting 4 into the box. 6 came out. With this result, what happens to Hajun's and Seoa's rules?

z-m-02-07.title: If pairs of 2 come out exactly, will groups of 3 come out exactly too?
z-m-02-07.topic: The rule for numbers of people that fit the conditions on how many are left over when grouped by 2s and by 3s
z-m-02-07.goal: Check by changing the number of people yourself that one grouping coming out exactly does not mean the other grouping does, then make many numbers of people that keep both conditions and state the rule of those numbers.
z-m-02-07.material: In gym class, let the number of students in our group be n. n is from 2 to 30. Soyul said, 'If nobody is left over when we make pairs of 2, nobody is left over when we make groups of 3 either.'
z-m-02-07.thinking.0: Testing directly whether it is always so
z-m-02-07.thinking.1: Finding many answers that keep both conditions together
z-m-02-07.thinking.2: Finding the rule in the answers you found
z-m-02-07.prereq.0: Counting by grouping into 2s and 3s with numbers up to 30 (Grade 2 level)
z-m-02-07.prereq.1: Finding out what is left over
z-m-02-07.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about what Soyul said?
z-m-02-07.s.s1.hint.0: Change the number of people to 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and make a table.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, for each number of people, write how many are left over when you make groups of 3.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.explain: 6 people come out exactly as 3 pairs of 2 and 2 groups of 3. But 10 people come out exactly as 5 pairs of 2, while in groups of 3 it is 3 groups with 1 person left over. Even if there are cases that fit, it is not 'always', and one case that breaks it is enough.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different numbers of students n for which nobody is left over when making pairs of 2, and exactly 1 person is left over when making groups of 3. (2 or more and 30 or less)
z-m-02-07.s.s2.hint.0: Increase the number of people one at a time, make pairs of 2 and groups of 3, and write the number left over in a table.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.hint.1: In the table, pick the numbers of people that satisfy the conditions in both rows.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 2 to 30.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 2 to 30.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Nobody is left over when making pairs of 2.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.fail.c2: 1 person is left over when making pairs of 2. The number of people has to come out exactly in pairs of 2.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.ok.c3: 1 person is left over when making groups of 3.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The number left over when making groups of 3 is not exactly 1.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.explain: The numbers of people that fit the conditions are 4, 10, 16, 22, 28. For example, 10 people are 5 pairs of 2, and in groups of 3 it is 3 groups with 1 left over. With 7 people, 1 is left over in pairs of 2, and with 12 people, nobody is left over in groups of 3.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.prompt: If you put the numbers of people you found side by side from the smallest, what rule do you see? Write what you see.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Calculate between the numbers you found one by one and write the difference between neighboring numbers.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether the differences are all the same, and think about where that size may have come from.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the numbers I found all go up by the same amount?
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you think about whether that amount is related to the number of people that comes out exactly in pairs of 2 and groups of 3 (6 people)?
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you guess whether the same rule will continue for numbers greater than 30?
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.model.0: They go up by 6, like 4, 10, 16, 22, 28. A group of 6 comes out exactly in pairs of 2 and in groups of 3, so adding 4 people to that seems to fit the conditions.
z-m-02-07.s.s2.because.model.1: Each time it goes from 4 to 10 to 16, 6 is added. It continues at the same interval, and after 28 I think it would be 34.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.o.a: Correct. If the number of people pairs up by twos, dividing by threes always works out too.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.r.a: Working out for one or two numbers of people does not mean it works for every number. They did not try dividing into threes while changing the number of people.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.o.b: Wrong. A number of people that divides exactly by twos always has some left over when divided by threes.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.r.b: 6 people divide exactly both by twos and by threes. Test whether there are cases with a remainder and cases without.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.o.c: It doesn't always work. You have to try dividing while changing the number of people.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.o.d: Correct. The bigger the group, the easier it is to divide exactly by threes.
z-m-02-07.s.s1.r.d: More people does not mean it divides exactly. You can find out by dividing directly for each number of people.

z-m-02-08.title: What can we say even if we do not know how many people there were at first?
z-m-02-08.topic: The result that adding and taking away changes make, whatever the starting number is
z-m-02-08.goal: Even without knowing the starting number, separate what you can say from what you cannot say using only the numbers of people who got on and off, and find what does not change by testing with several starting numbers.
z-m-02-08.material: A bus stopped at a bus stop, and 3 people got off and 5 people got on. We do not know how many people were on the bus at first. At other stops, nobody got on or off. We do not count the person driving the bus.
z-m-02-08.thinking.0: Separating information that is needed from information that is not
z-m-02-08.thinking.2: Checking a relationship that does not change with several examples
z-m-02-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you can say even without knowing how many people there were at first.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.hint.0: Pick the starting number any way you like, then find the number of people after some got off and some got on.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.hint.1: Put the starting number you picked and the number of people now side by side and compare.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.o.a: There are 2 more people on the bus now than at first
z-m-02-08.s.s1.o.b: There are 5 people on the bus now
z-m-02-08.s.s1.r.b: 5 is the number of people who got on. There were also people who were already on the bus, so you cannot say it is the same as the number of people now.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.o.c: There are fewer people on the bus now than at first
z-m-02-08.s.s1.r.c: Compare the people who got off and the people who got on. The 5 who got on are more than the 3 who got off.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.o.d: There are more people on the bus now than at first
z-m-02-08.s.s1.r.d: Even without knowing the starting number, you know that more people got on than got off.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.explain: The 5 who got on are 2 more than the 3 who got off. So whatever the starting number was, there are now 2 more than at first, and you can say it increased. To know how many people there are now, you need to know the starting number.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.acc.0: Saying there are 2 more than at first also includes the meaning that it increased from the start. You can choose the statement that it increased, too.
z-m-02-08.s.s1.acc.1: It is right that it increased from the start. How much it increased by (2 people) can also be said without knowing the starting number.
z-m-02-08.s.s2.prompt: From the story 'three people got off', what can we know about the number of people who were on the bus at first?
z-m-02-08.s.s2.hint.0: Draw whether 3 people could get off if there had been 2 people at first.
z-m-02-08.s.s2.hint.1: Change the starting number of people to 3, 2, 1 and check whether the story is possible.
z-m-02-08.s.s2.o.a: There were exactly 3 people at first
z-m-02-08.s.s2.r.a: 3 people getting off does not mean everyone got off. There may have been more.
z-m-02-08.s.s2.r.b: 8 is the number you get by adding the number who got off and the number who got on. It has nothing to do with the number of people who were there at first.
z-m-02-08.s.s2.o.c: We cannot know anything about the starting number of people
z-m-02-08.s.s2.r.c: People can get off only if they are there. If 3 people got off, how many at least must have been on the bus?
z-m-02-08.s.s2.o.d: There were 3 or more people at first
z-m-02-08.s.s2.explain: For 3 people to get off, there must have been at least 3 people on the bus. So the starting number of people is 3 or more. It is a condition that was hidden in the story.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.prompt: Let the starting number of people be a, and the number of people after 3 got off and 5 got on be b. Make 3 pairs (a, b) that fit the story, with different starting numbers. The starting number is 30 or less.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.hint.0: Pick a starting number of people and apply the number who got off and the number who got on in order.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write the starting number you picked and the number now side by side and check which numbers of people fit the story.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.ok.c1: The starting number of people is 3 or more and 30 or less.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.fail.c1: Use a starting number of people from 3 to 30. 3 people must be able to get off.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.ok.c2: The number of people now fits the story.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.fail.c2: The number of people after 3 got off and 5 got on does not fit. Apply the people who got off and the people who got on in order and count again.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.explain: If there were 3 people at first, there are 5 now; if 10, then 12; if 20, then 22. Even if the starting number is different, there are always 2 more now than at first. If there were 2 at first, 3 could not get off, so it would not make a story.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.prompt: Look at the (a, b) pairs you made side by side. Even when the starting number is different, what does not change?
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.hint.0: For each (a, b), write how different the two numbers are.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.hint.1: Check whether the differences you wrote are the same all three times.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: Even if the starting number is different, ...
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: In all three of my (a, b) pairs, is there a difference of the same size?
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the difference came from the 3 who got off and the 5 who got on?
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Can you also explain why a starting number of 2 will not work?
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.model.0: Whether there were 3, 10, or 20 people at first, there are always 2 more now than at first.
z-m-02-08.s.s3.because.model.1: The 5 who got on are 2 more than the 3 who got off, so no matter the starting number, there are always 2 more.
